scenes.title: The protocol
scenes.sub: Seven moments that decide your day, graded by evidence
scenes.say: Chapter nine. A practical protocol for the seven moments that decide your day, with every step graded by evidence.
A recall from chapter eight. What is the risk of a scheduled ideation slot for someone with MD?
scenes.sayA: It can become a sanctioned gateway into immersion. So cap it, write rather than just imagine, and track your total fantasy time.
scenes.a: It can become a gateway into immersion: cap it, write it, track it

scenes.head: The grades
items: A randomised trial in MD, or robust meta-analysis on the exact mechanism
Trials or meta-analyses in related problems, applied by analogy
Interviews, case reports, expert models, small studies
Reasoned inference that nobody has tested
scenes.say: First, the grades. A means a randomised trial in MD, or robust meta-analysis on the exact mechanism. B means trials or meta-analyses in related problems, like procrastination, addiction, insomnia or goal pursuit, applied by analogy. C means interviews, case reports, expert models, or small studies. D means reasoned inference that nobody has tested.

scenes.head: The only MD treatment trial (557 people, 8 weeks)
scenes.say: The backbone comes from the only MD treatment trial. It randomised 557 people to an eight-week online program of psychoeducation, motivation work, mindfulness and daily self-monitoring. Both program versions improved MD severity, frequency and functioning, with large effects. In the full program, 39 percent improved reliably, and 24 percent to a clinically significant degree, and the gains held at six months. A wait-list group, using willpower and online forums, did not improve. About 37 percent dropped out, and there was no placebo control.

scenes.head: (a) When the work gets uncomfortable
scenes.text: *Expect the moment, and reframe it*: the discomfort that triggers the urge is the same discomfort that signals ~learning~.
scenes.ev: B · learning research; D · as a reframe
scenes.say: Moment a: when the work gets uncomfortable and the urge hits. First, expect the moment, and reframe it. The discomfort that triggers the urge is the same discomfort that signals learning, because effortful practice feels worse and works better.

scenes.head: (a) Write one if-then plan. Rehearse it daily for 2 weeks.
items: I notice the urge to drift when the script or edit gets hard,
I say ‘urge’, take three breaths, and do the next two-minute step: one rough sentence, or one cut.
scenes.say: Second, write one if-then plan for this exact moment, and rehearse it aloud daily for two weeks. For example: if I notice the urge to drift when the script or edit gets hard, then I say urge, take three breaths, and do the next two-minute step: one rough sentence, or one cut. If-then plans improved goal attainment with an effect of 0.65 across 94 tests, and more with a strict if-then format, high motivation and rehearsal.

scenes.head: (a) Notice, name, return, log
scenes.say: Third, respond in three steps: notice, name, return. This non-judgmental awareness skill is the core of the MD trial, and a two-week mindfulness course separately reduced distracting thoughts and improved test scores. Don't try to force the thought away: across 31 studies, suppressed thoughts rebound. And don't berate yourself after a lapse. Then log every episode: start time, trigger, minutes lost, and what you did. Logging is the component that sped up gains in the trial.

scenes.head: (a) Make the task less aversive
items: Break it into micro-steps; finish one unit before switching
Take breaks when you need them, not on a rigid timer
Decide your break activity in advance: no music, no lying down
Pacing ritual? Competing response: seated, feet flat, hands on keyboard, 1 minute
scenes.say: Fourth, make the task less aversive. Break it into micro-steps, and finish one unit before switching, which reduces attention residue. Take breaks when you need them rather than on a rigid timer: a fixed 25 and 5 schedule raised fatigue without improving output. Decide your break activity in advance: no music, no lying down. And if pacing is part of your ritual, use a competing response. Notice the first sign, like reaching for earbuds or standing up to pace, then hold an incompatible posture for about a minute: seated, feet flat, hands on the keyboard. Habit reversal training reduced repetitive behaviours with a large effect.

scenes.head: (b) When your hand reaches for music
items: Make it unavailable, not just forbidden: apps blocked, earbuds away, phone in another room
Default to silence. Bridge with low pink noise or rain, then phase it out.
Expect the itch and earworms for days to weeks. Chew gum while writing.
Replace the hype track with a 5 to 10 minute walk, no audio
Run a 2-week test: words written or minutes on task, before vs after
scenes.say: Moment b: when your hand reaches for music. Make music unavailable, not just forbidden: streaming apps blocked during work, earbuds out of reach, and the phone in another room. In Somer's case study, a 25-year-old man who confined recreational internet to one late-evening hour cut his internet time by over 70 percent and his daydreaming by over 50. Default to silence, with low pink noise or rain only as a bridge you phase out. Expect the itch, and earworms, for days to weeks, and chew gum while writing. Replace the hype track with a brisk five to ten minute walk without audio. And run your own two-week test, words written or minutes on task, because your sense of what helps is unreliable.

scenes.head: (c) After something exciting happens
scenes.ev: D · trigger untested; B · if-then method
items: A short dhikr or word of thanks, if that fits you
Name the next concrete action, then do it or schedule it
Walk 5 minutes without audio. Never celebrate with music plus fantasy.
scenes.say: Moment c: after something exciting happens. Pre-commit to an if-then plan for good news. If I get exciting news, then I write one line about it, add a short dhikr or word of thanks if that fits me, name the next concrete action and either do it or schedule it, then walk five minutes without audio. Converting excitement into a process step matters, because imagining the process improves effort, while positive fantasy drains it. And never celebrate with music plus fantasy. It is the most amplified state the evidence describes.

scenes.head: (d) A success fantasy starts. Worked WOOP:
scenes.ev: B · g = 0.34; larger with a partner
items: Outcome (1 minute only): a channel that pays the bills
Obstacle, the inner one: ‘when editing gets boring, I escape into fantasy’
Plan: if editing gets boring, then I name it, breathe, and cut the next 10 seconds
scenes.say: Moment d: when a success fantasy starts. Give it a daily, five-minute, written home: WOOP. Here is a worked example. Wish: ten finished scripts this month. Outcome: picture the best result, a channel that pays the bills, for one minute only. Obstacle, the inner one: when editing gets boring, I escape into fantasy. Plan: if editing gets boring, then I name it, breathe, and cut the next ten seconds. Done with another person, the effect was larger, so review it weekly with an accountability partner.

scenes.head: (d) Instead of feeding the fantasy

items: Read the fantasy's theme as data: what need isn't met?
Small, shipped work with real feedback
Close each episode with one written line

scenes.say: Stop using success visualisation as motivation, and drop manifesting rituals. Positive fantasies predict fewer applications, lower pay and later depression. Start reading the fantasy's theme as data. Fame, recognition and competence fantasies point to needs that real life is not meeting yet. The real-world dose is small, shipped work that gets real feedback. And when a fantasy starts outside its slot, close it deliberately: write one line on where it stops, and leave nothing to be continued. Neutral interruption fits better than self-shaming.

scenes.head: (e) Before sleep and in idle time
items: Bed is for sleep only. Phone and earbuds out. Awake 20+ minutes? Get up.
Write tomorrow's to-do list 1 to 2 hours before bed
No music near bedtime: it brings sleep-disrupting earworms
Idle defaults: a walk, dhikr, a 2-minute task, or talking to someone
scenes.say: Moment e: before sleep and in idle time. Keep the bed for sleep only. Phones and earbuds stay out of the bedroom, and get up if you're still awake after about 20 minutes. Write tomorrow's to-do list one to two hours before bed: people who did fell asleep about nine minutes faster in a small study. In bed, use a 15-minute body scan, which shortened time to fall asleep in a trial of 232 adolescents. Keep music away from bedtime. Protect sleep for learning's sake: one night without sleep cut the ability to form new memories by about 40 percent. And pre-plan defaults for idle time: a walk without audio, dhikr, a two-minute task, or talking to someone.

scenes.head: (f) A daily system
items: 10 minutes of mindfulness; read the day's plan
60 to 120 minute creation block in silence, phone away
20 titles or 50 raw ideas, alone and fast
Stop every 5 to 10 minutes to reproduce; AI as tutor
scenes.say: Moment f: the daily system. In the morning, ten minutes of mindfulness, then read the day's plan. At the same time every day, a 60 to 120 minute creation block in silence, with one defined deliverable and the phone in another room. Daily, 20 titles or 50 raw ideas, generated alone and fast, with selection in a separate session. When learning, never watch more than five to ten minutes of a tutorial without stopping to reproduce it, and use AI as a tutor, not an answer machine. In the evening, your MD log, then tomorrow's plan.

scenes.head: (f) The weekly system
items: Edit deconstruction: rebuild 60 to 90 seconds, compare 3 editors
Peer exchange: swap and rank title and hook lists
Prediction log, checked against Test & Compare
One script section with no AI
Monthly: business experiment review + brand-asset audit
scenes.say: The weekly system. Franklin-style copywork on one top intro. An edit deconstruction: rebuild 60 to 90 seconds and compare three editors. A peer exchange where you swap and rank title and hook lists. A prediction log, checked against Test and Compare. One script section with no AI at all, to check the skill isn't fading. Two or three incubation walks with a loaded problem. A WOOP review with a partner. And monthly, a business experiment review and a brand-asset audit. Expect a two to three month ramp: forming a new daily habit took a median of 66 days. Set specific, hard goals, and keep progress visible.

scenes.head: (g) When to see a professional
items: Urgently: any thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Low mood or lost interest for 2+ weeks
Lifelong inattention that predates the daydreaming (possible ADHD)
Losing track of reality, or a history of trauma
Still losing deadlines or income after 4 to 8 weeks of self-help
scenes.say: Moment g: when to see a professional. Urgently, if you have any thoughts of suicide or self-harm. And for an assessment if you have low mood or lost interest for two weeks or more, intrusive thoughts or rituals that suggest OCD, lifelong inattention that predates the daydreaming, episodes of losing track of reality, or a history of trauma. Do the same if MD is still costing you deadlines or income after four to eight weeks of structured self-help.

scenes.head: (g) What to ask for
items: Assessment: MDS-16 and, if possible, the structured MD interview
Screening for depression, anxiety, OCD, ADHD, dissociation, with MD checked against ADHD
Targeted CBT: mindfulness, self-monitoring, motivation. Not generic talk.
Bring the papers: many clinicians don't know the term
A clinician comfortable with faith-consistent goals, like cutting music
scenes.say: Look for a clinical psychologist or CBT therapist, ideally experienced with dissociation or behavioural addictions. Ask for an assessment with the MDS-16 and, if possible, the structured MD interview. Ask for screening for depression, anxiety, OCD, ADHD and dissociation, with MD explicitly checked against ADHD. Ask for targeted treatment: CBT with mindfulness, self-monitoring and motivational work, because non-specific therapy is ineffective. Bring the papers, since many clinicians don't know the term. And if it matters to you, look for a clinician comfortable with faith-consistent goals, like cutting music. No medication has trial evidence for MD itself. Medication matters mainly for co-occurring conditions.

scenes.head: Evidence grades at a glance
items: Willpower and forums alone don't work
Bed for sleep; AI as tutor; peers pick ideas
Remove music cues entirely during work
scenes.say: Here are the grades at a glance. A: a daily self-monitoring log, mindfulness with notice, name, return, and the finding that willpower and forums alone don't work. B: rehearsed if-then plans, WOOP instead of success fantasies, silence for verbal work, the bed for sleep only, AI as a tutor, and letting peers and data pick your ideas. C: removing music cues entirely during work. And D: the excitement plan, and a capped ideation slot.
What is the one approach the MD trial showed does not work?
scenes.sayA: Willpower plus online forums. The wait-list group did not improve. Mindfulness plus daily self-monitoring did.
scenes.a: Willpower + forums. Mindfulness + daily self-monitoring worked.

scenes.say: Build the plan part of a WOOP for your music urge.
scenes.sayA: For example: if I reach for my earbuds during work, then I put them in the other room, breathe, and do one two-minute step in silence.
scenes.a: If I reach for earbuds during work, then I put them away, breathe, and do one 2-minute step in silence.

scenes.text: Last: a short, *mixed recap quiz* across every chapter.
scenes.say: Last: a short recap quiz that mixes every chapter, because mixing and testing beats rereading.
